$comment: What each published curb weight includes. The loader normalises every weight to one basis: full fuel, no driver. A tank filled to 90 % or an unstated fill widens the range upward; an unstated driver widens it downward by the largest driver allowance here (the EU's 75 kg).

definition.value: Weight 'in the state equipped as necessary for operation' (Road Transport Vehicle Act art. 40): full fuel, oil and coolant and the fixed equipment the vehicle needs; no occupants (55 kg per seat is added only for gross vehicle weight). Spare tyre, tools and other portable items are removed when the car is weighed (NALTEC examination rules).

sources.note: In Australia, Kerb Weight refers to the weight of a standard vehicle (with any factory-fitted options or accessories) with all of its key fluids (various oils and coolants) and with a full tank of fuel. This weight figure doesn’t include driver and passengers, luggage or cargo in the tray.

definition.note: carsales says options are not included; Mazda Australia says factory-fitted options are.

sources.title: Vehicle weights - What's the difference? — carsales.com.au, Alan Swanson, 2017-10-17
sources.note: DIN kerb weight is measured in a similar way to the Australian definition, although the fuel level is required to be 90 per cent of the tank's capacity. EU kerb weight is easily calculated from the DIN weight. Quite simply, EU kerb weight is always 75kg more than DIN. The European Union adds this 75kg ballast to account for a driver and a small amount of luggage.

definition.value: The figure prints no basis: it may be a DIN weight (no driver, 90 % fuel), an EU weight (75 kg driver) or a full-tank kerb weight. The loader keeps the printed figure and widens its range by the EU driver's 75 kg below and a part tank above.
definition.method: Covers the bases above; the largest driver allowance among them (EU, 75 kg) sets how far down the range goes.

fuelFill.method: No fill level is known for an unlabelled figure, so a part-filled tank is allowed for.
